summary: Water transport in plants for ages 7-8 (UK DfE Year 3 'Plants'): a first-hand, working-scientifically investigation in which children stand celery or a pale white flower in dyed water, watch the colour climb over hours, and slice the stem to see the tubes that carried it. The learning is threefold: the OBSERVATION (colour reaches the top, so water moved up), the PATHWAY (base/roots to stem to leaves and flowers, an upward route) and the METHOD itself (set up, wait, record over time, draw a labelled diagram). Keep the mechanism simple (water moves up through tiny tubes to the leaves) and do not formalise xylem/transpiration, which belong to later secondary science. A screen simulation can compress the slow process and let children run variations, but it is an untested scaffold paired with the real experiment, which supplies the actual evidence. In US NGSS there is no dedicated water-transport performance expectation at this grade; it sits near plant structure/function (1-LS1-1, 4-LS1-1) and plants' need for water (2-LS2-1, 5-LS1-1).
misconceptions: Thinking water moves DOWN or in all directions rather than being drawn upward from the base to the leaves.
Believing the stem 'sucks' water like drinking through a mouth, rather than water rising through fine tubes.
Assuming leaves get their water directly (e.g. from rain/air) rather than via transport up the stem.
Thinking the colour appearing in petals is the flower 'making' colour rather than dyed water arriving there.
Not connecting the observation to structure — missing that the stem contains tubes that carry the water.
Expecting the process to be instant rather than taking hours.

activities.title: Real coloured-water investigation (celery or white flower)
steps: Stand a stick of white celery with leaves on, or a pale white carnation, in a beaker of water dyed a bright colour (e.g. red or blue).
Before leaving it, write or say your plan: what will you look at, and when? Set up a before/after comparison and take a first photo or drawing.
Over several hours (or leave overnight), record what you see at intervals with photos or drawings, so the slow upward creep of colour is captured as evidence, not just a final result.
When the colour has risen, point out where the dye ended up (in the leaf veins / petals) and describe which way the water travelled.
Cut across the stem with scissors or a knife (with adult help) and use a hand lens to find the coloured dots or lines inside, the tiny tubes that carried the water.
Draw and label a diagram showing the path of the water: base/roots to stem to leaves and flowers.
activities.insight: Water is drawn upward from the base of the plant, through fine tubes inside the stem, all the way up to the leaves and flowers. Watching dyed water appear at the top is the evidence that this invisible, slow process happens.

activities.title: Compress and vary the investigation on screen
steps: Choose a specimen (white carnation or celery) and a dye colour, place it in the water, and drag a time slider forward to compress hours into seconds as the colour creeps up the stem and blooms into the petals or leaf edges.

Use a 'slice the stem' action to reveal the coloured dots inside (for a carnation stem these sit in a ring; in a celery stalk they sit in a curved row near the outer, ridged edge), the tiny tubes that carried the water, linking what you saw to the plant's structure.
Try a split-stem mode: put each half of the stem in a different colour and predict, then check, that the flower comes out two-toned.
Complete a label step: mark the water's path base to stem to leaves on the diagram.
activities.insight: Water moves up from the base through internal tubes to the leaves and flowers; varying the set-up (colours, split stem) shows the same pathway behaves predictably.

activities.title: Reference diagram: trace the path and the tubes
steps: Tap or point to the dyed petal and say what it tells you ('coloured water arrived here, it travelled up').
Tap or point to the stem cross-section and name what carries the water ('tiny tubes carry water up').
Tap or point to the base and say what happens there ('water enters here').
Using the diagram, retell the whole path in order: base/roots to stem to leaves and flowers.
activities.insight: A labelled picture of the dyed plant and stem cross-section fixes the pathway and the location of the transport tubes as a memory aid after the investigation.

activities.title: Check understanding of method and pathway
steps: Put the investigation steps in the right order (set up specimen in dyed water, record over time, observe the colour risen, slice the stem to see the tubes).
Draw the water's route on a plant outline from base to stem to leaves.
Answer: which way does water move through the plant, and where does the colour appear first and last?
Predict: if you split the stem and stand each half in a different colour, what will the flower look like?
activities.insight: Learners can state the direction of movement (upward), the ordered pathway, and the role of the internal tubes, and can predict a variation.

checkQuestion: Give the child a stick of white celery (leaves on), a beaker of water dyed bright red, a knife/scissors and a hand lens. Say: 'Set this up to find out HOW water moves through the plant, leave it, then show me what you found and where the water went. You can cut the stem to look inside.' Watch how they set it up, what they observe, and how they trace the path — don't tell them what to expect.
checkAnswer: Stands the celery in the red water, waits, and observes the red colour travelling UP the stem into the leaves; cutting the stem reveals red-stained tubes (vascular bundles) running through it. Concludes water travels from the bottom (roots end) UP the stem to the leaves, through tubes inside the stem. A good performance sets it up as a tracked observation and reads the path from root-end to leaves.
